Review:
Ok, so I WANT to give this watch 5 stars. My wife bought me this watch as a late birthday/Christmas gift about a month and a half ago. It came in and from the moment I took it out of the box, I could tell something wasn't right. It would do this weird Ghost touching thing, where it was almost like the watch would touch itself and it would be random, as if I was just randomly touching the display. It was very frustrating, but aside from that, the watch was great.
I reached out on the Mobvoi forums, where one of their support people told me to go ahead and do a warranty return, as I filmed a video of the watch doing what it was doing and their response was a very quick 'we'll send you a new one'.

So I did. I setup the return, packed everything back into the box and sent it off... I tracked the package to make sure it would get there and it did! But then came the wait...

3 weeks after the warranty ticket was put in and a bit more than 2 weeks after the return had been received by them, I finally got the replacement. Mind you, I didn't get a response from their support team about the issue until a little past the first week the return had been received by them, because I sent them an email about it, which seemed to have prompted a response.

The replacement is fantastic. As many have noted, the battery life leaves much to be desired, but I have the settings optimized and can get more than a full day of charge. The WearOS features on this watch work great and though many talk of it being laggy, I haven't really noticed. My last "watch" was a fitbit charge 2 that would hold a charge for more than a week, but also was limited as towards smart watch features. The Ticwatch though, has a beautiful screen, is nice and light and the ease of changing bands is great.

If anyone wants to try out a pretty good entry watch into the world of smart watches, this one is definitely a good and light on the wallet option.

So...

Pro's
- Lightweight
- Darned good display
- Wear OS
- Easy band changes
- VERY comfortable

Con's
- Company support? What is that? (I did get a replacement that works great, but I mean, response to messages and through the overall warranty process SHOULD have been faster, smoother and easier, especially for a watch that is very easy to REALLY, REALLY like)
- Battery life not as robust as maybe it should be.

Honestly, I really love this watch... The company's support though... cost it a star

I miss it at least once and have to scroll in the opposite direction each time. It's even worse if I get a string of text messages, as the most recent one is displayed right at the top, but then I need to scroll through a backlog of texts to get to the previous new ones. I'm not even really sure what determines how far back it pulls because it doesn't seem to follow a consistent pattern. One of the primary things I'd imagine people want a smart watch is for the ease of seeing notifications, this turns it into a chore just to check my texts. It's more convenient to just take my phone out. It doesn't even give you the courtesy of letting you know it's dying! Sure I get a little light saying it's at 20%, but from what I've seen depending on if I get any notifications that can get me anywhere from a few minutes to maybe 15-30 minutes before it turns off. I haven't gotten any additional notifications, or even a buzz to let me know, "Hey, I'm turning off now".

Touch Screen:
Despite having to swipe up or to the side multiple times for notifications due to it seemingly not detecting the swipe the way I want it to, I regularly look down to see that literally brushing against my shirt or a jacket over it managed to switch my watch face. Or that it dismissed a notification. Yes, there is a way to lock the screen by first tapping to "wake up" the display if it's idle, swiping down, tapping the brightness cog, and hitting the button, but is it really reasonable to have to do all of that to make sure that my SMARTwatch doesn't react to my shirt brushing against the face?

Display:
I don't know who designed the actual watch, but no matter what angle I look at it from, there's a pretty glaring distortion around the edges. It's honestly not the worst thing, but coming from a Pebble this was never an issue I experienced. If I'm paying over $100 for a small screen to connect to my watch that's purpose is to have me interact with it more than the actual phone to an extent, I don't think it's unreasonable to expect the display I'm looking at to be just as smooth as the phone it's supposed to be replacing. The image also shifts over every few minutes in either direction. I can only assume this is to prevent burn-in but it just makes the watch look like the screen is defective due to how sudden and rough the transition is.

Battery:
I didn't expect this to do anything near what my Pebble did, I charged that thing once every 3-4 days on average. But this one I end up needing to charge up almost 3 times a DAY with light use. If I try using the actually really awesome features such as being able to take a call or play music through the watch itself, that 3 times a day easily becomes 4-5 times.

Stability:
More than a handful of times now I've had the watchface distort when I get a notification in and it stays like this for 30 seconds to a minute completely unresponsive to touch or hitting the button. This doesn't seem to be linked to any particular watchface specifically, and like other issues that I've mentioned doesn't seem to follow a specific pattern. Sometimes I have a full day with no issues getting notifications.

I'd be interested to try the Ticwatch that runs on it's own OS to see how much of this is an Android Wear issue.

Review:
Before I get to the review, I’ll tell you a little bit about myself so you know how I use the watch. I’m an Emergency Medicine Doctor, beginner to intermediate runner and cyclist, and aspiring triathlete. I’ve owned the Forerunner 945 for about a month now, and prior to this I used the Garmin Fenix 5 and Apple watch 4 ( I hesitate to even include this because it’s really not a fitness watch). I am by no means a high level athlete, and I’m not going to qualify for the Boston anytime soon. I am, however, a data geek. I’m obsessed with wearables and the insights that they can provide us. For the sake of brevity, I’ll assume that anyone looking to purchase a 600 dollar watch knows what they are purchasing and has done a fair amount of research. My hope is to review some of those new features and help you make an informed decision.

Fit:

The Fenix 5 is built like a tank. Indestructible, heavy, but mostly annoying to wear. I found it difficult to sleep with the device on my wrist. The apple watch 4 was sleek, but I worried about cracking the screen during my workouts. The Forerunner 945 is just right. Sturdy, but significantly lighter than the Fenix 5. I wear this one all day and during sleep. My wrist is small to medium at 7 inches and I do not find the Forerunner too large by any stretch. It’s slightly less comfortable than the Apple watch for all day wear.

Appearance and performance:

I don't want you to convince yourself that this is going to look sharper than an Apple Watch. Apple has aesthetics down. In fact, the forerunner 945 has identical screen resolution to the Fenix 5. But edges appear sharper and brighter in actual use. The processor is noticeably faster from the Fenix 5 and navigating from screen to screen is a delight.

Features:

For fitness metrics, Garmin reigns supreme. It is so vastly superior to any other fitness watch on the market. This is a true multisport watch. Do not convince yourself that the Apple watch is a fitness watch. It is a smartwatch with fitness features. If all you need is cadence, speed, and distance, the Apple watch will do just fine. Buy an Apple Watch if you want a smartwatch. But if you’re looking at this review, you’re probably a dedicated runner, cyclist or triathlete. The amount of data on this little computer is absolutely incredible. From the very actionable lactate threshold feature, to the less actionable but interesting respiratory rate, this watch has something for everyone.

New Features:

If you're new to the Garmin ecosystem, I’d refer you to their website or First Beat to look at all the available features. However, if you’re looking to upgrade from a previous Garmin, i’ll give you a rundown of what’s new from the Fenix 5/Forerunner 935.

Music - Perhaps the biggest reason to upgrade. I use spotify, and found the integration to be absolutely seamless. Add Wifi network to watch, download playlists, connect wireless headphones (I use aftershokz air), play music. That’s literally it. Garmin kept it simple here. So simple that it’s easier to download music on the Forerunner 945 than the Apple watch.

Heat/altitude acclimation - This falls into the category of “interesting, but not sure what to do with it”. Garmin automatically accounts for external temperature by the use of local weather data (Not the watch itself), and gives you a percentage of acclimation. I live in Florida, so after the first week I was 100% acclimated and rarely fell below 95%. I’m not sure what to do with this. I don’t live or train at altitude, so I can not review that feature.

Training Focus - This feature surprised me. I really like the training focus graph. It’s very actionable if you polarize your training (As you should). I no longer have to depend on third party websites to see how well polarized my training is. If it’s time for a high intensity run, I do it.

Workout labels - You’re training effect now comes with a label (Base, Tempo, Vo2 max etc). This is a nice summary at the end of you’re workout. It keeps me in check. Often when I think I’m doing an easy effort, I stray into the tempo workout. This can only be seen after the fact, but it’s good for post run analysis.

Pulse oximetry - This falls into the category of “please remove this from the market immediately.” As a doctor, I hate this feature. Not because it’s a bad thing to include, but because it is terribly inaccurate, and the data is confusing for people. For a healthy adult, or even a sedentary adult without respiratory or cardiac problems (Asthma, COPD, etc), your normal pulse oximetry should always read near 100% at sea level. Regardless of whether you’re working out or not. I've compared this to hospital pulse oximeters and I can tell you the accuracy of this feature is so poor that I really wonder why they released it. The idea, from Garmins point of view, is that oximetry data can be used for altitude acclimation, sleep tracking, sleep apnea. Unfortunately, the error is at least 5-10% for any given reading. An adult with a pulse oximetry reading of 88% on room air would have severe respiratory problems. My watch will frequently tell me that I am 88%, only to check on a real pulse oximeter and see 99%. I turned this feature off and I recommend you do the same.

Body battery - I like this feature. It takes into account your sleep, stress, activity level, and VO2 max (Resilience against fatigue) and comes up with a number. Subjectively, I found my battery to line up with how I feel. I had a few drinks the other night, had a poor night’s sleep, and woke up to a body battery of 10%. If you had asked me how I felt before I looked at the number, I would have said a number around 10%. It’s a good tool for mindfulness and becoming aware of situations that drain you. I’m usually at 5% after a twelve hour shift in the Emergency Department.

Respiratory rate - Requires HR strap. Interesting, probably accurate ( Although I cannot confirm, using HRV makes sense in theory and the numbers seem to correlate with HR when plotted on a graph). This falls into the “interesting, but not actionable yet. Lots of potential in the future”. I can see Garmin doing some interesting things with this data (Lactate, ventilatory threshold improvements for example). Just not enough going on with it for prime time yet.

Updated and improved:

VO2 Max -Now takes heat into equation so your VO2 max doesn’t tank during the summer. Nice feature.

Training status - Also includes temp data for more accurate training load

Race predictor - New algorithm that relies on more factors than just VO2 max. It’s an improvement, but it’s still wildly optimistic I think.

Still needs improvement:

Wrist HR - Although Garmin claims that their new sensor is better, I found it to be equal to the Fenix 5, which is to say, not great, but acceptable at rest. This is a huge blow and the biggest reason I cannot give it five stars. In order for your data to mean anything, it depends on accurate HR data. I am not satisfied enough to run without my HR strap yet. Hopefully there will be improvements to come in the form of software updates. For now, get a chest strap.

Pulse oximetry - A real stain on otherwise well released product. Should remove feature entirely.

FTP auto detection- Never worked on my Fenix 5, still not working on my Forerunner 945. I ride with a power meter and HR belt so I don’t know where the issue is.

EKG - This is becoming standard now and it would be a nice health feature to add.

Text back features - Garmin still struggles in the smartwatch department. Notifications are nice, but you’re still tethered to your phone for text backs.

FAQ:

Do I need a chest HR monitor? Yes. If you’re going to splurge for the data options on the Forerunner 945 you should use a chest strap to enable all features, ensure accuracy of device.

What’s the difference between the Forerunner 945 and 245. The 245 is primarily a running watch. The forerunner 945 is a triathlon watch. The 245 has very limited data for cycling, and worse yet does not include lactate threshold for runners which is a huge let down. Falls into the category of "too expensive for a casual runner, not enough features for a dedicated runner".

Internet complaints I've come across when researching this product:

Pairing issues with music- Have not had a problem yet in a month of use. Pretty seamless for me.

Buttons “mushy” - Something I NEVER would have noticed if not for the internet. I guess they are a little soft? I don’t know. They feel exactly the same as the Fenix. Wouldn’t worry about it.

GPS inaccurate - GPS is on par with Fenix 5, Apple watch. Never had much variation between any of these. I run in a medium sized city with tall buildings and haven’t had any dropouts.

HR inaccurate - It’s true. It seems to be a continual struggle for smart watches (Except the Apple watch 4, who has figured out the magic formula). This is an optical HR monitor, so it depends on perfusion, which is variable throughout the day. To remedy, I still use a chest HR monitor which uses electrical conduction of the heart muscle and is extremely accurate.

Battery poor - I get like 4-5 days out of it and I run about thirty miles a week. I'm not sure if the people who complain about this run ultramarathons? But I can't really speak to any problems here.

Accessories I use:

AfterShokz Trekz Qir headphones. Love, love, love these headphones. They are the best. They work great with the Forerunner.

Garmin Tri HR monitor - Waterproof, durable, accurate chest strap.

Favero Assioma power pedals - Cheap, reliable.

Have fun out there!

Oh, I've even gone swimming with the warranty replacement watch and have had no issues to date.
/Update**

For a very long time, I have been looking for a Wear OS watch that I could use without it being tethered to a phone. The Mobvoi TicWatch Pro 4G/LTE is the answer to my prayers.

Previously, I thought I found the solution in the the LG Sport Watch, which was the flagship Wear OS watch with stand-alone SIM for phone and data. However, the LG was wrought with bugs and poor battery life. Not the TicWatch!

I found the watch to be indispensable and a decent replacement for my phone, especially when going on runs or other activities. I can figure it via Verizon Number Share. I was able to make and receive phone calls, instant message (I sideloaded Google Hangouts), text messages, etc. without having my phone nearby or even turned on. If you know where to look, you'll also be able to find the actual phone number for the watch, which people can call in addition to your phone's number.

I did go swimming with the watch and drained the speaker as I normally do. However, a few hours later, the watch ceased to work. Since I bought one of these for my wife, I verified that it was not a charging issue by using her watch on both chargers. My watch refused to turn on or respond.

I initiated a warranty claim on 2019-11-11. After some ridiculous amounts of back and forth emailing (some of the responses took 4 to 5 days), Mobvoi finally approved the warranty claim on 2019-11-26. However, for the warranty service, I was instructed to send the watch via postal mail to... Wait for it... China!

I got this really long mailing address string in one line:

"Room 901, 9th Floor, Tower A,New Zhongguan Shopping Center Office Building,No. 19 Zhongguancun street, Haidian district, Beijing,China Mobvoi 4008838390"

This is beyond ridiculous. I have never mailed anything to China. Is this the correct address format? I think I need to put carriage returns somewhere, right. Anyhow, I'll have to go to the post office and mail the watch for warranty service. It's been already over 2 weeks since I started a claim, I'm now wondering how long it'll be before I will be made whole.

Review:
I purchased this to use in conjuction with the Lose It! app (on my iPhone). It is the least expensive activity tracker that you can pair with Lose It!. I would commend this to you if you are interested in owning an activity/sleep tracker but you are not willing to fork out about $100 to try one. I was apprehensive about buying any activity tracker because none of them consistently get stellar reviews (most average in the 3.5 stars range). I've never used anything like this before so I don't have that bit of comparative experience to add. Here are my findings:

1. This works very well with the Lose It! app. If you are interested in seeing exactly how much (or how little) you move about during a day, this will help you establish a baseline. I also enjoy using the activity tracker to motivate me to add a few more steps to each day. If you are using the Lose It! app, you will see your steps taken along with the calories burned AND a calorie bonus if you are active enough.

2. There are two Misfit apps. Both do different things. I am grateful for another reviewer pointing out that the regular Misfit app is going to give me information regarding activity and sleep. You can view by the day, week, or month if you would like to see trends. The Misfit app periodically will sync your device with your phone, or you can manually sync as well. The Misfit Link app can be used to manage multiple Misfit devices, as the Misfit Link can be used to control music, take selfies, etc. I am only using it as an activity tracker right now and I only have the one device, so I'll reserve comment on the rest. The Misfit LInk app is also how you configure how you want to use your device--mine shows activity progress first, then the time of day. I can tag activity time by one long press. The Misfit Link app will also show battery life on your device.

3. It took about a day to become familiar with the device and able to use it easily. I still don't like the clock as much as my watch, but I don't want two things on my wrist and I don't want this on my other wrist either. Sigh. First world problems.

4. It comes with a clip that easily attaches to your clothing. I've also clipped it to my watchband. The clip is sturdy and works well. I did purchase watchbands for this tracker because I feared that I would leave it on my clothing and wash it eventurally. I purchased these bands. [[ASIN:B00Y6XSME8 GL-Sail(TM) Set 6 Colors Replacement Bands Wristband Strap with Clasps for Misfit Flash(Pack of 6) (6PCS For Misfit Flash)]]

5. I have not tested the claims of water resistance. I am saving that as an emergency safety measure.

6. I appreciate that I don't have to recharge anything. I also enjoy the fact that this tracks my activity without being in range of my phone.

7. The Misfit LInk will share information with the Apple Health Kit.

I think the this is a excellent value for the money. If you are new to the wearable activity tracker market, I think this is a good entry point. I would buy this again.

Update: At the 3 week mark, my device would not sync with my phone. I contacted Misfit and I received a timely response (a few hours). I went through a list of things that they recommended to sync. The last thing was the recommendation to replace my battery. I thought this was unnecessary as my phone had been reporting 100% batttery life prior to the syncing issue. I removed the battery and then put the same battery back in. This solved the problem. I also did not lose any data from the time that my device did not sync despite having removed the battery. I have not had a repeat of the problem. I am still pleased with the performance of this device as an activity tracker. I also received two follow up emails from Misfit to make sure everything was working ok.

Review:
When I was researching activity tracker/ smartwatches online, I was confused by the lukewarm reviews of the Vivoactive 3 - very few people seemed to really love the watch, but it offered good functionality at a low price and didn't seem to have anything particularly wrong with it (at least compared to the also-new Fitbit Ionic). After owning one for 10 days now, I still like it, but I kind of share the lukewarm sentiment I encountered in other reviews, so hopefully I can now explain why.

I previously had a Fitbit Charge HR, which was cheaper and did a reasonable job of tracking sleep and heart rate, but didn't offer much beyond the basics, and besides, it looked kind of clunky and was starting to fall apart. What I was hoping to find was a GPS HR tracker that looked good enough to wear with a suit, that offered better running metrics and offered a bit more in the way of smartwatch features without being too pricey.

In these respects, the Vivoactive 3 does fit the bill. It looks great (most people don't even notice that it's digital, much less that it's a running watch), it tracks my runs and other activities well and - as far as I can tell - it offers all the functionality of the more expensive Forerunner 235 and most of the features of the still-more expensive Fenix 5. Plus new features like stress measurement and GaminPay!

Well... that's all more or less true. But. For one thing GarminPay isn't set up yet and even when it is, it won't work with every bank and at every retailer. I don't think I'd actually use it much even if it was functioning, but given that it isn't, it can't really be viewed as an improvement, and if it's important to you to be able to pay with your watch, the Fitbit Ionic or Apple watch are probably safer choices. Other options in the same price range mostly offer built-in music storage which the Vivoactive does not. Also, the battery life is advertised as being 7 days - this may be true if bluetooth is off and you don't use the watch at all, but as far as the real world is concerned, 7 days is kind of a fiction. If you don't switch bluetooth off, it will last about 24 hours. If you do, you need to go in and switch it on every time you want to sync the watch (not actually a big task, but still irritating). At the moment I'm getting about 4 days out of each charge with moderate use. And stress measurement? Some reviews have claimed that this is subjectively accurate, but that hasn't been my experience. Every time I get up to make a cup of tea, the resulting increase in heart rate is listed as 'med' or 'high' stress. And I'm British, so that's quite a lot of the day. If I'm sitting down and writing a difficult e-mail or giving a presentation, it generally shows low stress. Perhaps it needs to learn a bit more (it has now managed to cut out any walking of more than a few minutes), but so far it's been pretty wildly off.

There are other irritations - sleep tracking has failed on 4 of the 10 days, the side swipe button (which be useful in winter with gloves but otherwise isn't much use) can be triggered by loose clothing and start skipping through menus and actually reset the time once, the 'move' reminders can be irritating. Even features I expected to be top notch have struggled at times - for example I did a run yesterday starting up 6th avenue in midtown New York, and the GPS showed me going along 6 1/2th avenue (yes, that is a real thing). Sure, I was weaving around tourists, but the difference is about 200ft and it really is supposed to be more accurate than that. To be fair, it was on target the rest of the way and has been close enough on my other runs.

As mentioned above, some of its competitors seem to offer more functions for the non-runner. An Apple watch, Samsung or Fitbit will offer more apps, built-in music storage and in some cases personal coaching sessions which are lacking from the Vivoactive 3 (although you can create workout plans on Garmin Connect and put them on the watch). Personally, I use a phone for most apps, don't have wireless headphones and don't need in-watch coaching. Similarly, the more expensive garmin products offer more advanced metrics, more accurate GPS, open swimming tracking, etc and so offer more for the more serious athlete.

Having said all of that, this is still a good watch and some of its flaws will be fixed in time as patches are released, more apps become available on Connect IQ, etc. It is easy to use as a regular watch, it's light and comfortable and looks great. It offers most of the features of the Fenix 5 at half the cost, and all the fitness features you'd find on anything cheaper. You can reply to text notification while out jogging (although only with a standard reply) and might one day be able to buy your post-run rehydration with Garmin Pay. I can't resist using it to check the weather at every opportunity, and I've always wanted a watch with an in-built compass. It is leagues ahead of the Fitbit I used to own, although Fitbits have moved on in that time too.

So in conclusion, it is a good watch that has its flaws and is surrounded by competitors with potentially superior features. If you are a serious runnner/ cyclist/ triathlete, etc you probably need a greater range of metrics and activity apps (although the Vivoactive 3 can be paired with accessories quite easily to cover some of this data). If you are into fitness more generally and want something to track gym/ cardio sessions, the new Fitbit probably has you covered and offers a little bit more for the same price. But if you exercise outdoors at a casual to intermediate level and want a watch that covers all your fitness needs while looking great in the office and future-proofing you with smartwatch capabilities, the Vivoactive 3 is the watch for you.

Among the top features I wanted was Apple Healthkit integration. Fitbit absolutely refuses to play nice with Apple and Garmin promises to fill that bill. I went for my first run with my Vivoactive the night after I received it and it quickly locked on to the satellite while stretching. Two subsequent runs since then had the same quick satellite acquisition.

I train with teenagers to run a half marathon. With the kids, we run intervals. What fitbit described as an interval timer was not an interval timer. The Garmin gave me a noticeable vibration at 6 minutes when it was time to walk and again after a minute when it was time to run. The fitbit would have just vibrated every 6 minutes which is not useful. If you are going to run intervals, you may as well do it right.

This is also a much nicer looking watch than the Surge or any of the current Fitbit offerings in my opinion. I also think it looks much better than my Apple Watch.

The Garmin also has many features that pretty much make me think I will wear my Apple Watch less often. The Surge only let me read text messages. The Vivoactive pretty much gives me all the notifications that my iPhone does. A nice feature is that these can be muted during a workout or set that only phone calls give an alert.

I would have gave this 5 stars, but I’m kind of wary of the battery life claims. After the initial charge to 100%, I wore it to bed to track sleep and the battery drained to 82% for a 6 hour sleep. Googling this I read that turning the watch off and back on again would correct this. I’ve worn the watch for 12 hours today and and ran almost an hour and a half using GPS and I’m at 69% which I can live with I suppose.

Review: I received this as an early Christmas gift from Amazon and am extremely pleased with it. I found it paired easily with my Galaxy S4. I just downloaded the Gear Fit Manager app (in Google Play Store) and it set up easily. Some people have commented that it is confusing to set up and use but I found it very easy (I'm used to the Android operating system). I personally like all the options for set up and they seem intuitive to me. The Gear Fit Manager allows me to add additional apps under "Notifications" so I can get their alerts in addition to the standard ones that come with the Gear for phone, texts, email, alarms, calendar appointments.  For instance, I use K9 Mail for my business emails and was able to add that app so that I get separate alerts for my business emails.  I can then easily see who is trying to reach me without digging out my phone from my pocket or handbag. Review:
This is my first smart watch, so please keep this in mind as you read my review. I connected this watch to my Google Pixel 4a (Android OS). Compiled pros and cons are the end.

Back in the days when phones were becoming more than phones, there was a general type of phone called a 'feature phone.' It came pre-loaded with a variety of popular apps. But you were locked in to those apps by the firmware. You could not add or remove any of them. Such is the case with with this smart watch.

Set-up was straight forward. It requires installation of its own app, 'DaFit', from the Google Play store. The watch started up indicating about 70% charge, which is appropriate for storage. At my rate of usage, from a full charge, I found the watch easily maintained a charge for more than 24 hours. While the app indicates the watch is connected after set-up, I recommend reviewing its presence and confirming settings in your phone's Bluetooth connected devices panel, too.

The straps came unattached to the watch, but thanks to a small post on the spring-loaded pins, I was able to quickly attach them to the watch body...just have a decent fingernail available.

Like most smart watches I've seen, the form factor is a bit on the big size as a compromise to the amount of information it attempts to display on the watch face. My issue there with this watch, given its size, is the three control buttons which protrude significantly from the circumference of the watch. The correct orientation is to wear the watch with these control buttons pointing toward the wrist joint so the opposing hand can easily access them. However, because of their size they quickly begin irritating the base of your hand as your wrist flexes throughout the day, such as when typing on a keyboard (I'm a desk jockey so that is most of my day). I eventually turned the watch around moving it to my right arm (I'm left handed so this is actually preferred even though the control buttons are no longer in the correct orientation for access by my left hand). For right-handed users, this presents a problem as the preferred wrist to wear it on would be the left.However, keeping it on the left wrist but turning the watch 180 degrees so as to have the buttons away from the wrist joint would then cause the display to be upside down. A firmware upgrade allowing a 180 degree re-orientation of the display and generic assignable buttons could address this as well as the issue of left-handed users for whom button irritation as above is not an issue, but would want the buttons easily accessible while wearing it on their right arm.

I was eager to read my incoming text messages on the watch instead of pulling out my phone, unlocking it, and reading them there. The problem here, though, is that only those texts which were sent from a phone number displayed only as a number, and not in my named contacts would be sent to my watch (!). No matter how many times I had my family members (named contacts in my address book) send me text, they would never appear in the watch, but only in my phone's messaging app and phone notifications. This is a big fail!

I use Google Fit to track a lot of my health metrics and was pleased to see steps as measured by the watch could be sent to my Google Fit app. But, the watch also has the capability of measuring pulse, blood pressure (BP), and oxygen saturation (O2Sat). These measurement are not sent to Google Fit, and only the most recent seven are stored on the watch. With respect to blood pressure measurements: DON'T USE IT for any reason! Sure, any medical measurement from such a device should be treated with suspicion...but it can suggest you may want to take a blood pressure reading from a better quality, more reliable device such as a true sphygmomanometer. But, even at this level of credibility, this watch's BP measurement sensor is very inaccurate. I found the diastolic (upper reading) to be off by ~ -30 mmHg and the systolic to be off by ~ -10mmHg. This could easily give someone a false sense of security if they never had their BP checked by another device. I do have to track my BP and know what my reading should be. This watch's BP measurement was nowhere near what my true BP is. It's almost as if it picked two numbers at random and displayed them as my BP.

Overall, I think this smartwatch, even for the price, has the opportunity to be a bit smarter.

Pros
>Pliable soft silicone strap provides for secure but comfortable fit
>Maintains a charge for more than 24 hours of average use
>Good screen resolution and brightness (adjustable)
>Good sensor touch on screen
>A decent variety of interchangeable watch faces including one which allows you to import your own graphic/image as the backdrop
>Step counter integrates with Google Fit

Cons
>Wired proprietary charger. If it breaks or you lose it, too bad. A USB charging cable isn't a viable replacement (recommend re-design for wireless charging)
>Very inaccurate BP measurement to the point of being worthless
>While it measures steps, pulse, blood pressure, and O2 saturation, it only sends step metrics to Google Fit, even though Google Fit can receive all of these data points.
>For text messages, only those which display as numbers in your phone's texting app, i.e. those not in your contacts/address book, appear on the watch. Text messages from your named contacts for some odd reason are not sent to the watch.
>Accessing the panels to review pulse, BP, and O2 saturation also initiate a new measurement. This is not needed, especially since you may only want to review passed measurements, not necessarily obtain a new measurement. Recommending designing a start button on these panels to initiate a new measurement.
>Because of the form factor, the side of the watch with the control buttons needs to point away from the wrist to avoid irritation which detracts from the ability of the opposing hand to properly access those buttons.
>Weather data does not appear at times with a message "Please check Bluetooth connection" even though Bluetooth connection is confirmed as text messages noted above and other notifications appear.

Review:
The sensor of my expensive name brand smart watch fell off so I wanted to replace it with something that is not so expensive. On sale, this watch was only $40 so I went for it.

It came in a box with a charger. The charger has two little charging contacts that magnetize to the back of the watch. It charges quickly and lasts about three days with regular use.

The watch app is Da Fit. The app is user friendly. There are a bunch of watch faces you can change to. It has a lot of the normal features: steps, sleep, heart rate, workout, etc. You can set your step goal and sync with Google Fit. I didn't sync to it so I don't know if it's accurate. That's the app, now to the watch.

It is a big watch for me. It's 1.75" by 1.5". I had to change the band to one I had because the one that came with it was too long to fit any of the holes. End to end when attached to the watch is 10.25".

The actual function of the watch was not that great. Calls were fine. They were clear and connected quickly. I never could figure out the messaging. A message would show up, but I didn't figure out which icon was messaging so I couldn't read them again. The icon page was intense so I left it alone.

The steps were way off. I know my phone is accurate because it was synced with my first watch and they were always the same and my steps also match the treadmill. But the this watch recorded at least twice the amount of steps. I tested it and it was recording my arm movement. So if you like to have a lot of steps without putting the work in, this watch is for you!

There weren't many workouts to choose from although I thought it was great that skipping and badminton are two of the choices. Also, the heart rate function does not work. My heart rate gets very high when I work out (185 bpm) and every time I checked, the watch showed 78 to 109 bpm.

I did like the fact that you could set it to remind you to drink water. Sometimes I need that little nudge.

The weather was accurate and you can use your watch to be the shutter for your phone camera although I could never open the icon to test it.

So, I would recommend this inexpensive Rawnaig Smart Watch if you just want a lot of faces to choose from, a timepiece, the ability to make and receive calls and a few other features. If you also want an accurate workout watch or an easy watch to message with or the ability show your own pictures, this is not the watch. That's not to say that there are other inexpensive smart watches that would work nicely.

[[VIDEOID:9b6258d2767bd2e6a0b2ab190bea9b07]] (Update) The sleep monitoring function didn’t work at first, but after updating and rebooting a few times it works now. Text messages and some notifications don’t display, but I think that has something to do with iMessage. Will update if anything changes. (End update)

You can disable “raise to wake” with the touch of a button (on screen). To me, that’s huge. Most of these smart watches will always turn on when you move your wrist. Not only does that kill the battery, but it’s really annoying when you’re trying to sleep and use the sleep monitor function, or in a movie theater, or in any situation like that. Not a problem with this watch.

The AMOLED screen is really bright and more awesome than I expected. I’ll never use a non AMOLED watch again. The difference is pretty noticeable. The screen is sharper, brighter, and looks just amazing. Non AMOLED watches now look like children’s toys to me. I’m using the blue digital face with black background and it’s so bright and sharp it looks really high tech, or like something out of TRON. There is also an AOD option, or always on display. You can choose either a white on black digital or clock face time display that will always stay on, also showing date and step count. It’s simpler and a little dimmer, so doesn’t eat as much battery, but still lowers standby time a little. So far it hasn’t been too noticeable a difference. You can even set a start and end time for it to activate. If you turn off the “raise to wake” function, it pretty much becomes like a normal watch, until you turn it on via the side button. Sweet.

As far as the accuracies of the apps, I can’t say. None of these smart watches are super accurate, but good enough to get a base line and compare health statistics day to day. This one has GPS so I’d imagine it’s a bit more accurate than others for certain things. Just be sure to turn on weather and choose notifications after set up. None of it is turned on by default. The phone app is easy to use and has more options than some others.

The rubber watch band is really smooth and comfortable, but not the best looking thing to me. Thankfully, most of the smart watches of this type (if not all) use the same type of bands, so I just switched it out with a metal one I had. There are spring loaded pins in them that you can pull open with a fingernail or small screwdriver. Changing them takes less than a minute.

So far, this is the only smart watch that does everything I want it to. On top of that, it has the AMOLED screen. The only downside I’ve seen so far is that it’s not capable of wireless charging, so my wireless charging stands are useless for this. But it does come with a magnetic contact pad charger which connects to USB, and I guess that’s good enough. Will update with any issues, but I think I’ve finally found a smart watch worth using.

I'm a tech-geek who has been watching the smart-watch segment for years.I travel a lot so battery life is crucial for me. I am also an avid runner, hiker, and cyclist who likes to track health.

Quick note: Heart Rate monitor NOT built into watch. Its a band that goes around your upper waist and connects wirelessly to the watch.If I had known this before purchasing, I would have saved myself $50 and went without it.

Setup: EASY! Within 5 minutes I had my Vivoactive synced up to the Garmin Connect App on my Galaxy S4 Android phone. By default, all Apps (Facebook, text messages, calendar reminders, work email, Gmail) relay the messages to the watch. Range is also good. I live in a split level home and it doesn't loose connection unless I am outside (50 feet away). It gives me a gentle "buzz" and message saying that its no longer connected to my phone.

Everyday use: I love the fact that everytime I get a notification that I can just look at my wrist rather than picking up my phone. If its important, I'll pick up my phone to respond but for everything else, I just carry on. While driving, typing at work, carrying groceries, or sitting in a meeting, it has made it much more convenient to keep up with my digital life. I also tested its water resistance by taking a shower with it this morning without any problems.

Battery/Screen brightness: Its been 24 hours and I still have 89% of my battery life left. That includes me configuring it, learning all the screens/options/settings, and showing it off. I am hoping for 1 week+ of battery life. Part of that I think is due to the screen. At first it seemed dim but that's because I am used to a phone or laptop screen which this watch is not designed to work like. As long as there is some light in the room I can see the screen just fine. If I can't see it then I just hit the backlight button. No its not cell phone bright but it doesn't need to be. If you have used a digital watch with a backlight this is what you will expect. If I had to choose great battery life, or a bright screen, I'd choose battery life every time.

Comfort/Style: It's light and very comfortable. While running I built up some sweat under the band but nothing unusual compared to other watches. Size is on par with your average digital watch and looks very normal and stylish. I have normal size wrists for a guy and it doesn't look bulky. It also doesn't stand out as most people don't notice unless I point it out.It doesn't have any sharp points or angles so I have had no problems with clothing getting snagged.

Comparison with Fitbit One: I used my Fitbit for step counting and sleep monitoring. I used both of them together for the first 24 hours and the results were very similar which I didn't expect since the Fitbit is warn at my hip and watch is obviously on the wrist. Both were identical for sleep monitoring and the Vivoactive was only 75 steps higher than the Fitbit at the 10,000 step mark. I talk with my hands so I figured these numbers might be way off but that wasn't the case.

Pro's
* Lightweight
*Good size. Not big and bulky but big enough to read everything without needing to pull my wrist to my face
* Comfortable
*Stylish/Doesn't stand out. I work in a professional environment (Suit) so I am happy that its not an eye sore.
*Battery life. 89% battery life left after 24 hours
* Easy to setup, configure, and pair with my phone and the Garmin Connect App

The TOZO S1 Smartwatch is a promising smartwatch with no doubt many upgrades to come. There are many things I love about this watch.

1. The 240x240 resolution display, while in comparison to a phone is low quality, on the comfortably sized, 1.54 inch screen, is very sharp and bright and looks almost better than some name brand watches.

3. The fit of the watch is odd, but maybe just for me. I'm somewhere between two sizing holes, so one is too tight and the other is too loose, but I don't blame this on TOZO, just my personal experience.

Overall, this watch is amazing. At only $39.98 USD (at the time of review), this watch not only holds its own, but is in someway better than some name brand watches that I have seen. There are flaws, yes, but I guarantee if you but this watch, it will satisfy every need you may have. This watch is in my daily routine and will only leave when the next one comes out. TOZO is not your average cheap electronic company. They are above that. Their products are some of the best I've ever used, even despite the price. Don't Doubt, Go TOZO.

After using and comparing both units side by side, I decided to return the Nuvi 760 and keep the RoadMate 1470.

Here are what I like about the RoadMate 1470:

- Bigger, brighter, more colorful screen
- Very helpful lane assist (I live in Southern California, I see it works at all highway exits and interchanges here. I haven't tested it in other parts of the country yet). The Nuvi does not have this feature
- Bell/chime before each turn. The Nuvi does not have this
- Much more flexible routing options (Can exclude a maneuver or detour 3/5/9 miles from a route)
- Free lifetime traffic with the traffic link device(I got the traffic link for free). You have to pay about $40 a year for traffic with the Nuvi
- Useful Onetouch feature
- Much louder internal speaker
- Lighter, slimmer

Here are what I liked about the Nuvi 760:

- Faster re-routing/recalculation (Both units give very similar routes, though)
- More sensitive touch screen. The RoadMate screen sometimes takes a few presses to recognize/react (noticeably the back arrow button)
- Sturdier/more durable in build quality
- A little better text to speech (More voices to choose from and the voice quality sounds a little clearer/less synthesized). The 1470 has only one voice and the lady's voice sounds kinda nasal but very understandable though
- Faster processor, making the unit perform faster. The RoadMate seems sluggish sometimes

The Nuvi 760 has some other features like bluetooth, mp3 player, picture viewer, FM transmitter, but none of them work well enough to be useful. After having used the RoadMate for 3 weeks, I still like it better and think I made the right decision to keep it intead of the Nuvi 760.

Review:
First - Im not new to fitness watches. Ive used other Garmin watches, Fitbit watches and 2 Polar watches. I wanted to love this watch, but I might end up returning it. Although its advertised as 5 day battery life in standard watch mode, it only lasts me about 2 1/2 without EVER putting it in GPS workout mode. Just straight watch mode.
The GPS when you use it kills battery 25% per hour. So a fully charged, straight off the charger and out for a run/walk will be completely dead in 4 hours if your using GPS during your run/walk/bike ride, etc.
The band itself is very soft and comfortable, but does cause irritation (itchy red spots) on the back side of my wrist where the metal clasp is.
Flight (stairs) counting is hit or miss on accuracy. I was out camping this weekend literally sitting in a campsite, and got 9 flights of stairs while doing so during day 1st day?? (yes- it was a level campsite literally at sea level (ocean front), no hills anywhere around, just a flat spot of ground where tent/fire-pit/picnic table sat and I got 9 flights of stairs sitting in a camp chair in front of fire, with a few trips back and forth to cooler/picnic table a few feet away). Other days, while at work I take multiple flights of stairs everyday (3 floors up 3 floors down) and will somedays record flights accurately, and somedays not give me any flights of stairs at all.
GPS 80% of time finds the satellites within 1 min. BUT the other 20% of time, Im standing around waiting seriously 15-20 minutes in wide open sky area for it to find the satellites (wait...wait...wait) which annoys my running/biking partners.
As I stated, Ive owned other GPS Garmin watches, and also FitBits, and Polars, and really really wanted to love this watch. So its not that Im unfamiliar with how to use them, or don't know GPS sucks battery life (it does on all watches), But I think Im gonna return it. I can't trust its accuracy (steps and flights of stairs while sitting in a campground not walking or climbing hills), its battery life (2 1/2 days without workout mode being used, 4 hours or less when workout mode with GPS), or that it will even find GPS satellites within a timely fashion (i.e. less then 15-20 minutes).
If your purchasing strictly as your first fitness watch and want to use as a motivation tool to get up and move and track your steps each day - its a great watch in those regards and it will motivate you to get up and move!. If your an experienced fitness watch user, and expect it to work with similar accuracy of other fitness watches, move along.
I think if Garmin beefed up the battery similar to the GarminActive, added Glonass, and a true altimeter for measuring elevation gain/loss, it would solve all 3 of these issues.

Garmin Vivoactive 3 is exactly what I am looking for in a smart watch/fitness watch, and more importantly it looks and feels stylish in its classic circular form and light weight design.

Before I talk about its smart and fitness features, I will briefly talk about its display. Display has good enough clarify for a watch. Its always on display is a huge positive compared to Fitbit and apple watch. Outdoor visibility of its display is great and definitely better than other OLED displays due to its specific display technology. On paper its display is inferior to Apple watch, Fitbit Ionic and other wear os watches (formerly Android Wear) in Pixel density and colors, but don't let it stop you from buying Vivoactive 3 as its diplay is perfectly fine and always on display more than makes up for its other shortcomings. I like it even better than other high resolution displays for its positive impact on battery life.

Let's get less important things out of the way first, and that is its smart features. It does what it supposed to do as a smart watch. It notifies me for the applications I have selected in Garmin connect app on my phone. I only keep text and phone call notifications on, and may be couple other important apps to avoid constant vibrations on my wrist. It does notifications very well. Just to clarify I have connected it to my Pixel 2 XL, and I have no connection issues. The only issue I have found is with phone call notifications, where notification persists even after I pickup or decline a call directly on my phone, but other than that it works perfectly fine.

Now I will get to more important part of the watch, and that is fitness. When it comes to fitness, I like everything about Vivoactive 3. The amount of detailed data you get on your workouts is well worth it. My most favorite part of all is being able to see what heart rate zone I am training in during my exercise. It does everything fitbit and other smart watches do and lot more. You get usual matrices like daily steps count, active and inactive calories, floors count, heart rate data and then some extras like weekly intensity minutes, VO2 Max, Fitness age, Stress level etc. You also get move reminders. I like the way I can look at it and tell how long I have been inactive. It reminds you when the red bar of inactivity reaches halfway and then again when it reaches all the way. If you want to varify its accuracy, there are plenty of you tube videos, and based on all reputable sources data you get is fairly accurate.

Three things I want to mention on accuracy though.

- Heart rate: I like the fact that it can connect to external ANT+ chest strap for accurate heart rate monitoring during exercises in which wrist heart rate monitors are not that reliable. I connect it to Garmin Heart rate monitor during my strength training, and I am very happy with the results I get, which by the way only costs $20.

- Floor Count: As many reviewers have mentioned, floor count on vivoactive 3 is very disappointing. Sometimes, it counts fairly well and sometimes it doesn't register it at all. Something to keep in mind.

- GPS: GPS signal is very quick to acquire and accurate. The route it tracks even detects the slightest variations in route (running on right side of the street vs running on left side of the street)

It tracks outdoor run/walk and indoor treadmill run well with plenty of data to review. Rep counting on strength training is surprisingly accurate. It even identifies the type of exercise based on the arm movement. It even identified me doing push ups every time I tried, which is very surprising given the fact that there is very little wrist movement in it. Starting and stopping sets and advancing in a next set is done by double tapping the screen which is very convenient.

All the activities and workouts are saved in Garmin Connect app with plenty of data. It even tells your fitness age based on your VO2 Max.

I can't believe I waited this long to buy my first Garmin Watch, and I am positive that Vivoactive 3 won't be my last Garmin Watch either. I did not come across any of the bugs other users have encountered during my first week of usage. It's been few months since its release and it seems like Garmin has fixed most of its bugs.

SUMMARY:

- Very light weight design, which looks classy in its circular form (I specifically love my slate version)
- Fairly accurate heart rate monitor, and activity and workout tracking
- Ability to connect to external heart rate sensor is a huge plus in my opinion
- Somewhat hit or miss floor count
- Smart watch/smart notifications features are minimal but very useful and reliable
- Advanced dynamics on workout data are very informative

All in all, Vivoactive 3 is a solid smart watch for fitness enthusiastics and everyone who want to live and lead healthy life. I highly recommend it..

This is my first smart watch. This one has a few built-in features -- clock, timer, alarms, fitness tracking, sleep tracking, phone dialer, and notifications from your phone, etc. More advanced features cannot be added later [other watches let you install apps to add features such as maps].

The voice assistant is interesting. It could be useful, but tends to get confused and doesn't always do what is asked of it. Trying to set alarms proved to be trouble. It would set alarms, but not cancel them without cancelling ALL the alarms. Even then, the voice assistant still thought the alarms existed after they were deleted.

There is a companion app that gets installed on your Android phone (or iPhone if that's what you have). It seems rather generic. Other smart watch companies use what looks like the same app with different icons, colors and branding. I was hoping that any of these apps would work, just so I had freedom to choose something different. Unfortunately, the FitCloudPro app was the only one what works with this watch.

From the app, you can choose the "dial" (watch face style) to be installed and used on the watch. There is a large library of options to choose from, but some of the dials in the Amazon photos are mysteriously absent. Many dials are just hideous, some are too busy, some too simple. I was able to find a few that I like, and I've settled on one. The watch itself holds five "watch faces" in memory. Yes, it is confusing that the watch calls them something different than the app. Out of those five slots, only one of them can be modified to hold your selected dial from the app. If you had hopes of loading five of your favorites and swapping between then, you will be disappointed.

The most useful feature of this smart watch is the notifications from your phone. You can leave your phone in your pocket or nearby, and the watch will display notifications from whatever apps you choose. I have it set up to show SMS/MMS text messages, Whatsapp messages, and Facebook Messenger messages. Everything else is turned off. This is a nifty feature, but the space allowed for messages is rather small and the type is too large. Any long messages get truncated. I wish there was a way to reduce the type size so more of the message could be seen, or maybe have a way to scroll long messages.

When I first started using the watch, I began to have problems playing music through my car stereo. I could control playback from the watch, my phone would show that music was playing through my car stereo, the stereo would show that the phone was connected, but there would be no sound. Once I removed the app and reinstalled, Bluetooth audio returned to normal. I'm not sure what the cause of this was, but reinstalling the app was the solution for me. It has been fine for a few weeks now.

The screen itself is bright and crisp. The user interface took some getting used to -- mostly trial and error.

The extra watch band is a nice bonus.

This is a great smart watch. It is chockful of useful features and handily syncs to your smartphone so you can get instant notifications about texts, FB messages, and phone calls. It can also track your heart rate through the sensors under the watch face, a blood oxygen meter that shines a red light into your wrist, and most popular of all tracks your number of steps. It is basically a miniature basic smartphone interface in the shape of a watch.

The build quality of the watch is great, with an HD screen, speaker, microphone, and a decent battery life. The screen has vivid colors, fine details, and an adjustable brightness that's visible even under full sunlight. The speaker is loud for such a small device and the microphone is sensitive. I can pick up calls and talk through the watch with relative ease and clarity. There are also 10 interesting preloaded songs, such as Baby by Justin Bieber and another by Adele with which you can test the sound. It also lasts a long time between charges and the battery life is about 1 week of daily use (occasional phone calls, mostly in sleep mode) before needing to be recharged.

The software is well designed, with everything polished and working smoothly. The accompanying SmartPro App is intuitive to use and has the more detailed features that the watch can't do by itself, such as downloading custom wallpapers. You can download and upload wallpapers through Bluetooth, and also switch between different wallpapers with a twist of the watch knob. Most of the built in functions of the watch are intuitive to use. The only feature I can't seem to get to work is the sleep monitor as it never seems to start even when I go to sleep.

Overall, this is great smartwatch that can pick up calls, read and send messages, and remotely control your music playing devices.

Review:
I needed a Wear OS watch to go with my Google Pixel 3 smartphone. I tried ones from Fossil, Diesel and even a Tiezen one from Samsung, but I always came back to the TicWatch Pro. The reviews maligned the device and the choice by the developers to have their own health app in place of the Google Fit, so I was cautious. I decided to purchase this and am very glad I did.

This thing is pretty innovative in how it preserves battery. It has 2 screens a full color Amoled one and a FSTN digital one overlaying that. When the Amoled screen times out it goes back the the "Essential Mode" screen which is to say the low powered digital screen. After setup and the normal time for Wear OS to index and calm down, I am getting some pretty good battery life. With raise and touch to wake on, wifi/bluetooth, NFC and GPS all on I am getting over 2 days of use, thanks in part to the timeout to the essential mode screen. When I leave always on, I still get a day and a half of use. Additionally if I put it into Essential Only mode, it lasts for weeks. Additionally I found that if I go into a workout the essential screen shows workout data that is germain to my activity (Very cool and battery saving)

Despite having an older processor, this thing is much faster than the Fossil gen 4's I used. Additionally a very cool touch that the other watches did not have is a speaker (So you can take calls dick tracy style) and a magnetometer so you can use compass apps and have better walking directions with the Google Maps app.

Lastly the band is really really nice with leather on the top and stitched into a rubber band on the back. The band smells of fine leather when you take it out of the packaging, and remains handsome in day to day use. This is a fine looking watch as well and wears well on larger wrists.

If there is one criticism, it is the one you hear everywhere. I wish they let you change the right to left swipe gesture to pick Google Fit over their Mobvoi health app, or at least allow the choice, but in practice their app has been non intrusive and really not bad at all. I even use it a little more than Google Fit, so maybe they are on to something.

All in all I really love this watch and I am very critical on products and will return something that does not work for me. I cant wait to see what Mobvoi can do with the newer Snapdraggon chipsets. They have certainly made the most of the gen it has. Also did I mention the price. Got this for a black Friday price of $199 and got a free activity tracker with it, that also turned out to be really excellent and something my wife wears all the time (Quite a feat). I will check back in 6 months to add more to the review but I think I am still going to be happy. Did I mention I recently came from the Apple camp and had Apple Watches since their inception? If I can be happy with this watch, then I think anyone can. Great piece of kit.

1) You can set data fields from 0-4 to view. This is important because you only want to glance at your watch while swimming, biking, running and you want to get the most important info to you. On the Polar, you can have four data fields but they are harder to read while running, etc.
2) The heart rate monitor is very comfortable to wear and accurate. The Polar is thicker and not as accurate when running (I've had my HR from 0-220 while running!) The Polar didn't stay on in the pool unless I made it really really tight. Ultimately it wasn't worth swimming with the HRM on in the pool.
3) Garmin Connect website easy to use, set up, download, share, etc. It's also important to know that the website includes elevation changes so you can see why you slowed down with increased heart rate while climbing an 8% grade.
4) Customer service was fantastic and quick. Being a guy, I didn't want to read the manual. Once I couldn't figure out how to download the information I called them and they were able to help right away. I dealt with Polar several times. Average response time to email reply was a few days and their response was to usually call them.
5) For swimmers, this is a must. It will keep track of distance without having to touch the "lap" button on your turns. I push the lap button while resting and it knew that I took a break. The watch kept track of my freestyle stroke and when switched to breast stroke, I didn't have to do anything; it just automatically happened.

Overall it's a great watch. Yes it is slightly bigger than the Polar but it's smaller than the older Garmin 310XT. No matter your sport, this is a great watch to have.

Review:
Many of you are like me (or were like me), searching for your very first smart watch. I came across the Ticwatch S while browsing Amazon's Prime Day Deals. They were going for a very good price at the time, so I discussed smart watches in general with a couple co-workers who own SW's and if they are actually worth purchasing. After a few conversations, I decided to take the leap and purchase one. Excited when it came in, I retired my G-Shock Tough Solar and set-up my new Ticwatch S Smartwatch (Knight Model) with my Samsung S8 Edge. The packaging was designed excellently and very minimalist (Watch, USB Magnetic Charging Cable, and Paperwork). It does not come with a wall socket USB adapter/charger, but I have plenty lying around and they are pretty inexpensive anyhow. Set-up was extremely easy and only took minutes. Uses the latest Android Wear OS too, which is a plus.
The watch is extremely lightweight, which worried me on how tough this thing is gonna be. I've been wearing it for almost two weeks now and I've gotta say, it's taken some good abuse and is still standing strong (I'm no construction worker, but I work a pretty physically demanding full time job). At this moment, the watch face doesn't have a single scratch or mar on it and I've bumped it into counters, corners, walls, etc. Whatever they used to manufacture the watch face is pretty tough material. I just worked on some plumbing for my Father, wearing this watch, and it's still holding up (even after getting wet, see photo). Yes, this watch is waterproof to an extent. I haven't swam with it, but I've washed dishes, been outside during a rainstorm, accidently wore it in the shower a couple times, and used a cleaning water bucket with it on. No issues so far. Today, I was just outside playing sports in a rainstorm for an hour and the watch performed as it should. So it's a tough smart watch, it's proven itself to me so far. Now I'm not saying this is a G-Shock or Iron Man, but it's a smart watch and a moderately priced one at that. So you really have to ask yourself what you want in a watch here. Which comes to my headline question, do you need or should you get a smart watch?

Here's some things I find handy about owning a smart watch:
-Notifications on the fly, even when you're away from your phone (I leave my phone on silent,so the watch alerts me to calls, texts, emails, etc with a light vibration), never miss an important text or call or message (even from Facebook, Insta, Twitter, etc)
-Better to glance at your watch while driving than pick up your smartphone, it's safer in my opinion
-Useful apps (Android Wear Operating System) Google Fit, Alarm, Find my phone, Flashlight, and much more
-Google Fit will measure your heartbeat, steps, exercise and send data to your phone
-Works great if you use Google Voice Assist too (I do)
-Is compatible with Google Maps (will actually show a little map on the watch), GPS Built in
-Speaker and Microphone built in (Voice to text is very accurate)
-Answer phone calls, texts, messages with a tap on your wrist. Select music, pause music, play music, all controlled on your wrist.
-I like I can be in another room, while my phone is charging and still have communication with my phone.
-Tells Current Time, Weather, News, etc.

In short, don't expect a freaking full fledged smartphone on your wrist, but a smartwatch adds a level of convenience I found to be worth while.

Now that I've gone over owning a smart watch, here are some pros and cons of this watch in general (Ticwatch S Smartwatch-Knight):
PROS:
-Lightweight
-Durable
-Good, responsive screen and motion controls
-Great selection of Ticwatch digital watch face designs
-Durable straps (I workout with this watch on, no issues, sweat resistant)
-Great Value
-Warranty (Always a breath of relief)
-Good, clear speaker and microphone
-Charges quickly, easy connect and disconnect (Magnetic)
-Charge lasts one and one half to a couple days depending on use.

CONS:
-Not compatible with Fitbit (Not Mobvoi's fault, Fitbit does not allow smartwatches to be compatible with their app, it's annoying)
-Not the prettiest watch, just a plain black, semi-sporty looking watch. Maybe simple is elegant?
-Not the largest amount of built-in memory, but it does have cloud storage

So that's my two coin on this watch and owning a smart watch in general. If you decide to take the leap, this is a great start for your journey into smart watches. You will not be disappointed in this watch. Especially at the price tag for this watch.

Review:
First off, you should be leery of any company that offers free stuff in exchange for 5-star review as is the case here. I'm not taking the bait. Instead, here is an honest review of this watch which I received as a Christmas gift (the reason I'm not a verified buyer).

Basics: Like all decent watches it tells time. The calendar is nice though it is unable to sync to your smartphone events. Battery life for the limited time I had it seemed quite good - it could make it nearly two days with pretty regular use before it needed to be recharged. It includes a leather and rubber band which I found easy to swap out.

Setup: Syncing to my iPhone was relatively simple after downloading the required app. I read the entire manual. It offers some basic startup guidance.

Multiple Display options are appreciated and they are visually pretty neat.

Features I tested over 2 weeks:
1. Health: BP is a complete joke, though I'm not sure anyone expects this to work. I sure hope not. I'm borderline hypertensive and was getting readings <100/50 mmHg. HR seems okay at times but also wildly inaccurate at other times - (e.g., 90 bpm when a manual check was over 120 bpm during exercise). Did not try the pedometer.

2. Sport Mode: One of the reasons I wanted this was to replace my trusty old Garmin with something that could both track my run and allow me the ability to change music on the fly. Short story - on a run today I know to be exactly 8 miles I wore both watches - the Garmin came in at 8.03 miles whereas this registered at 8.3 miles. 0.3 miles is outside standard deviation and just too inaccurate for me to rely upon. Also, it counts up from 1 during the run but didn't seem to match my mile markers (e.g., flashed "11" at 6.21 miles). This just served as an annoyance. I don't understand what this was about.

3. Notifications: here is an area I was actually fairly pleased. I would occasionally need to power cycle the watch for it to start receiving push notifications (even though connected via Bluetooth) but for the most part, any calls and push notifications would show on the phone as expected.

4. Music Control: Again, this worked pretty well. Volume Up/Down and Forward/Backward worked great. Only the song title displays and is limited to about 14 characters. If it's any longer, it will not scroll to show the entire name, nor is the artist shown. Not a huge deal but worth mentioning.

5. Find Phone: I work in IT and spent a few hours trying to get this to work with my iPhone. It doesn't.

6. Remote Capture: works but only using the Smart Watch app. It would be useful to have a countdown before the picture is snapped. As is, if you're in the picture, it will be of you touching your watch to trigger the photo.

7. Weather: So far, in two weeks I've seen exactly TWO temperatures displayed - 17°F and 21°F. I'm no meteorologist but believe our temperatures fluctuate a great deal more than that. Right now it registers 21°F but happens to be 40°F. This is one of my bigger disappointments.

8. Compass: I didn't spend much time with this but it didn't seem nearly as accurate as my phone. It sort bounced around and seemed to have trouble locking in on an orientation with me standing completely still.

9. It vibrates at random times for no apparent reason (at least not that I've been able to figure out). Customization, aside from the various "themes", is pretty limited.

Overall, I kept making excuses as to why this watch was worth keeping but have simply run out of reasons. For something that claims to be a "Smart" device, it is far from it. It seems like a product that was in beta testing and released without being fully functional or accurate. Sure, the price is remarkable for the supposed features it boasts but if only a small fraction actually work as designed, you'll have to make up your own mind about whether that equates to a good value.
